title: Prime-field discrete logarithms in randomized polynomial time
formal: Does there exist one uniform classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\), and integers \(C,c\ge1\), such that \(A\) halts within \(C(L+1)^c\) steps on every binary input of length \(L\) and every sequence of its random bits, and has the following correctness property? For every prime \(p\), every generator \(g\) of the multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^{\times}\), and every \(h\in\mathbb F_p^{\times}\), given the binary encoding of \((p,g,h)\) specified below, it outputs the unique integer \(x\in\{0,\ldots,p-2\}\) satisfying \(g^x\equiv h\pmod p\) with probability at least \(2/3\).
definitions: The field \(\mathbb F_p\) consists of residues \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\) with addition and multiplication modulo the prime \(p\). Its multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^{\times}\) is \(\{1,\ldots,p-1\}\) with multiplication modulo \(p\). The promise that \(g\) is a generator means that \(g^0,g^1,\ldots,g^{p-2}\), reduced modulo \(p\), list these \(p-1\) residues without repetition; hence the requested exponent exists and is unique. Each input integer is represented by its ordinary base-two expansion \(\operatorname{bin}(a)\), without leading zeros and with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\). Writing \(\ell(a)=|\operatorname{bin}(a)|\), set \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^{\ell(a)}0\operatorname{bin}(a)\). The complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(p)\operatorname{code}(g)\operatorname{code}(h)\), with \(p\) prime and \(1\le g,h<p\). Its length \(L=2(\ell(p)+\ell(g)+\ell(h))+3\) is \(\Theta(\log_2 p)\) on promised inputs. A successful output is exactly \(\operatorname{bin}(x)\); any different output or a designated failure symbol is unsuccessful. For \(p=2\), the sole promised pair is \(g=h=1\) and the answer is \(x=0\). The machine has a fixed finite program, fixed finite alphabets, a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes and an output tape; each transition costs one step, and any random transition reads one fresh independent fair bit. The time bound includes input processing, bit arithmetic, random-bit generation, output and all preprocessing. The same \(A,C,c\) work for every input, with no advice, oracle, precomputed table or supplied factorization of \(p-1\). Arbitrary classical computations on the concrete binary residues are permitted, not just generic group operations. Malformed encodings may be rejected as failure; on well-formed triples outside the mathematical promise, only the global time bound is required. The success guarantee is separately for each promised triple, over the machine’s coins, not over a distribution of primes or targets. The question concerns the multiplicative group of a prime field; additive groups, extension fields and elliptic-curve groups are different models.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of \(A,C,c\) with both the all-input, all-random-sequence time bound and the per-promised-input success guarantee, or a Lean-checked proof that no such triple exists. Equivalently, a negative answer must prove that every machine obeying some global polynomial clock has a promised input on which its probability of outputting the required exponent is less than \(2/3\). Failure of a particular algorithm, an average-case conjecture for a selected prime distribution, or a lower bound restricted to generic group operations does not establish this negation. A quantum algorithm, success only for selected prime families, or a bound polynomial in \(p\) rather than its bit length does not meet the positive target.
why: Discrete logarithms expose a basic gap between efficient modular exponentiation and our ability to invert it. A uniform classical polynomial-time solver would defeat the corresponding finite-field discrete-logarithm assumptions and solve computational Diffie–Hellman in this setting. An unrestricted impossibility proof would establish a fundamental classical lower bound for a concrete arithmetic problem already solvable in quantum polynomial time.

importance.reason: One of the principal unresolved number-theoretic algorithmic problems, with direct connections to cryptography, index calculus, and quantum speedups.

progress.text: Prime-field NFS methods achieve heuristic subexponential estimates, described precisely in the cited 2008 survey. Those historical estimates are distinct from proven expected-time bounds and from a lower bound against arbitrary algorithms.
Shor supplies a quantum polynomial-time discrete-logarithm algorithm; §6 of the inspected manuscript uses the same prime-field and supplied-generator mathematical problem.
Shoup’s Theorem 1 proves a generic-encoding lower bound parameterized by the largest prime divisor of the group order. It does not apply to unrestricted computation on concrete residues.

Kleinjung and Wesolowski’s fixed-characteristic theorem appears in the inspected 18 November 2019 version and the 2022 JAMS article. The expected-time bound and extension-degree parameter do not give a prime-field polynomial-bit algorithm.

Discrete Logarithm Factory analyzes shared preprocessing for a constant proportion of fields of a given approximate size and degree, with individual-target costs separated. Its publisher abstract and full introduction were checked.

Lido’s Finite Fields and Their Applications article concerns small characteristic. The inspected preprint’s Theorem 1.1 requires \(d>p\), so its quasipolynomial guarantee does not settle the prime-field question.

Wu and coauthors explicitly assume worst-case classical hardness of prime-field DLP in a new quantum-complexity preprint. Version 1 remains the sole version on 14 September; its conditional reduction is not a resolution of the assumption.

status_note: The original number-theory survey leaves the classical prime-field problem open. The same generator-input problem is explicitly assumed classically hard in Wu et al., arXiv:2608.15545v1 of 16 August 2026, still its sole version on 14 September. The reviewed 2026 small-characteristic publication and quantum results do not resolve this target. A bounded later-work search found no matching classical polynomial-time solution or unrestricted impossibility proof; source proofs and new conditional reductions were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: For a supplied \(g\) and exponent \(x\), modular exponentiation takes time polynomial in their bit lengths. Inverting this operation would reveal the shared value \(g^{ab}\) from \(g,g^a,g^b\) in the corresponding Diffie–Hellman setting. This implication does not identify discrete-logarithm hardness with every Diffie–Hellman or encryption-security assumption. The card asks a worst-case algorithmic question; a negative answer alone does not prove average-case hardness for a cryptographic parameter distribution.

Candidate answers are efficiently verifiable by checking \(0\le x\le p-2\) and \(g^x\equiv h\pmod p\). Thus, as an elementary consequence of verification, existence of the stated bounded-error algorithm is equivalent to existence of a Las Vegas solver that is never wrong and has a uniform polynomial expected running-time bound on every promised input. Independent verified repetition has bounded expected cost in one direction; truncation at three times an expected-time bound gives success at least \(2/3\) by Markov’s inequality in the other. This does not require every run of a Las Vegas solver to terminate, only probability-one termination and finite expected cost.

Schirokauer’s survey gives a conjectured expected-time NFS bound of the form \(\exp(O((\ln p)^{1/3}(\ln\ln p)^{2/3}))\) in the prime-field regime. This is a heuristic complexity analysis, not an unconditional polynomial-time theorem or an unrestricted lower bound. The displayed scale grows faster than every fixed power of \(\log p\). The 2024 Discrete Logarithm Factory paper separately studies costs shared across fields and targets; any such preprocessing must still fit this card’s complete single-input budget.

Shoup’s lower bound concerns randomly encoded group elements. If \(q\) is the largest prime divisor of a cyclic group’s order, constant success requires \(\Omega(\sqrt q)\) generic group operations in that model. His parameter \(q\) is not the field characteristic \(p\); for this card the group order is \(p-1\). The theorem averages over the random encoding, exponent and algorithm coins. It does not exclude algorithms that use the actual integer residues and their arithmetic structure.

Kleinjung and Wesolowski’s Theorem 1.1 gives expected time \((p d)^{2\log_2 d+O(1)}\) for the multiplicative group of \(\mathbb F_{p^d}\). For fixed \(p\) and growing extension degree \(d\), this is quasipolynomial in the input size. Substituting \(d=1\) supplies at most a polynomial-in-\(p\) guarantee, not the requested polynomial in \(\log p\). The occurrence of the product \(p d\) in their bound must not be confused with the field order \(p^d\).

Lido’s paper, published in March 2026, also proves a quasipolynomial expected-time theorem in small characteristic. In the inspected version its hypothesis is explicitly \(d>p\) for a field of size \(p^d\), excluding the growing prime-field family with \(d=1\). The source’s field-regime restriction remains part of the theorem even though all these problems share the name discrete logarithm.

Shor’s polynomial-time algorithm uses quantum computation. Wu and coauthors’ August 2026 preprint uses the same prime-field generator-input problem as an explicit classical-hardness assumption for a claim about estimating outputs of adaptive shallow quantum circuits. That assumption is not a proved classical lower bound; the reduction and its quantum resource claims were not independently verified in this review.

sentences: Given a prime p, a generator g and a nonzero residue h, the task is to recover the unique exponent x between zero and p minus two with g to the x congruent to h modulo p.
The question asks whether one classical randomized algorithm can do this in polynomial time in the full binary input length on every promised input.
All preprocessing is charged, and the running-time bound must hold for every random sequence while success is at least two thirds separately on each instance.
This would invert a basic arithmetic operation used in finite-field cryptography and match a known quantum capability.
A complete Lean proof must establish the algorithm or rule out all algorithms in this model; generic lower bounds, quantum algorithms and small-characteristic extension-field results do not suffice.
